chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal said: A man narrated to us from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman; and Muhammad ibn Ya'qub also narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from some of his companions, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Fudayl ibn Yasar, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"A man is not killed for the blood of his son, and the son is killed for the blood of his father if he killed his father; and a man does not inherit from another man if he killed him, even if it was accidental."

Because this report is mursal (disconnected chain), and despite that, it is possible that the reasoning behind it is what our Sheikh, Abu 'Abdillah Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man, said: that a man does not inherit from the man he killed accidentally from his diya (blood money), but he inherits from him from what is beyond the diya; and the one who kills intentionally inherits nothing, neither from the diya nor from other wealth. And with this interpretation, he reconciles between the two hadiths, and this is a close opinion, and that which confirms this interpretation is what was narrated:

key_terms.دِيَة: Blood money or compensation for killing
key_terms.مُرْسَل: A hadith with a disconnected chain of narrators

ai.seo_question: Does a killer inherit from their victim in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* articulates the principle of *ghulum* (exclusion of the killer from inheritance), with the commentary by Shaykh al-Tusi highlighting a nuanced Shia interpretation: while an intentional killer forfeits all inheritance, an accidental killer may retain a share of the estate excluding the *diya* (blood money). This distinction, attributed to Al-Numan, resolves apparent contradictions in hadith literature by differentiating between the source of the inheritance, thereby reinforcing the juristic consensus on the moral and legal disqualification of the killer.
